This research aims to stimulate a more nuanced discussion about the ethical implications of misinformation detection systems, with the ultimate goal of promoting a more just society. Link prediction in knowledge graphs is a crucial task in knowledge graph completion, which has been extensively researched in recent years. Most existing methods focus on learning entity representations by capturing the relationships between entities, but they often overlook the semantic connections between entities. To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach called Generalized Relation Learning with Semantic Correlation Awareness (GRL-SCA). This method utilizes a graph convolutional network to learn entity representations by incorporating both direct and indirect semantic correlations. The direct correlations are derived from the co-occurrence of entities in relation triples, while the indirect correlations are obtained by aggregating the semantic information of neighboring entities. To further enhance the performance, we introduce a contrastive loss function that encourages the semantic representations of related entities to be close together. Experimental results on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. The code and pre-trained models are available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhengrui-ai/GRSCA. In the context of machine learning, differential privacy is a crucial tool for safeguarding sensitive data. However, its application is often hindered by the substantial computational costs associated with the introduction of noise. This study delves into the potential of using optimization techniques to mitigate these costs, specifically examining the interplay between the noise's impact and the model's generalization capabilities. We investigate the effectiveness of two optimization methods, Stochastic Gradient Descent and Adam, in conjunction with two noise types, Gaussian and Laplace, and two privacy levels, $\epsilon$ and $\delta$. Furthermore, we discovered that the noise's impact is more pronounced when the privacy level is set to $\delta=10^{-6}$ compared to $\delta=10^{-8}$. Additionally, we observed that the noise's effect on the model's performance is more significant when the privacy level is set to $\epsilon=1$ compared to $\epsilon=10$. This study also highlights the potential of using regularization techniques, specifically L1 and L2 regularization, to enhance the model's generalization capabilities. We demonstrate that the model's performance is significantly improved when L1 regularization is employed, specifically when the noise's impact is more pronounced. This study provides valuable insights into the potential of using optimization techniques to mitigate the noise's impact and improve the model's generalization capabilities. We believe that the findings of this study will contribute to the development of more effective optimization methods for differential privacy. Additionally, we suggest that visualizations can be used to support code writing, particularly for complex tasks. The meta-filter enables the model to adapt to new tasks by selecting relevant data, while the dynamic alignment technique ensures that the model learns from the selected data. This approach is achieved through a two-stage process: first, we utilize a meta-filter to select relevant data, and then we employ dynamic alignment to learn from the selected data. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method, which outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches. The application of deep learning in medical imaging has been hindered by the scarcity of annotated data, particularly in low-resource environments. This issue is compounded by the challenge of adapting models trained on one dataset to another, due to differences in data distribution. This paper proposes a novel approach to unsupervised domain adaptation for medical image classification, utilizing a combination of disentangled representations and graph convolutional networks. By decoupling domain-invariant features from domain-specific characteristics, the model can effectively adapt to new domains. This is achieved through a novel disentanglement loss function that encourages the model to extract domain-agnostic features. Additionally, the model incorporates a graph convolutional network to capture domain-specific information. Experimental results on the BraTS dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods. transfer capabilities of multilingual BERT models, specifically focusing on how
they handle out-of-vocabulary words in target languages. We propose a novel
approach that involves two stages: first, aligning the target language with the
source language using a cross-lingual similarity metric, and then using the
aligned target language to make predictions. Our results demonstrate that this
two-stage approach outperforms a single-stage model, and we also show that the
aligned target language retains valuable information from the source language. 
Furthermore, we found that the performance of the two-stage model is highly
dependent on the quality of the cross-lingual similarity metric used for
alignment. This research provides new insights into the cross-lingual abilities of
multilingual BERT models, and we hope that it will inspire further research into
the mechanisms behind these models. The code and data used in this study are
available at https://github.com/nyu-dvl/First-Align-then-Predict.

Reinforcement learning (RL) has been successfully applied to numerous tasks, but its practical applications are often hindered by the need for extensive training data. To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach, temporal shift reinforcement learning (TSRL), which enables RL agents to adapt to new environments with minimal additional training. By leveraging a temporal shift module, TSRL can transfer knowledge from a source environment to a target environment, even when the target environment's dynamics are unknown. This approach is particularly effective in scenarios where the target environment's dynamics are similar to those of the source environment, as demonstrated through experiments on multiple MuJoCo tasks. The results show that TSRL can achieve comparable performance to that of a model-trained agent, while requiring significantly less data from the target environment, and even outperforms a model-free agent in certain scenarios. In the realm of generative modeling, disentangled representation learning has garnered significant attention, with the primary objective of isolating distinct factors of variation. However, the majority of existing methods rely on extensive unlabeled datasets, which can be impractical to obtain. This paper presents a novel semi-supervised approach to disentangled representation learning, leveraging a StyleGAN-based framework. By utilizing a single, limited-labeled dataset, the proposed method effectively decouples the latent space into two distinct components: one corresponding to the target label and the other encompassing the remaining factors of variation. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in achieving disentanglement. Furthermore, the proposed method exhibits robustness to the presence of confounding factors, such as label noise and domain shifts. Additionally, MSRL can be easily adapted to work with distributed RL systems that use multiple GPUs, which can further reduce data transfer requirements. Overall, MSRL provides a flexible and efficient solution for distributed RL that can be applied to a wide range of tasks. In this research, we introduce a novel approach to spatial assembly, combining reinforcement learning, self-play, and tree search to generate complex structures. Our proposed method, Spatial Assembly Network (SAN), is a generative model that learns to assemble components into cohesive spatial arrangements. SAN is composed of three key components: a spatial encoder, a policy network, and a tree search module. The spatial encoder extracts spatial features from a given component, while the policy network generates a sequence of actions to assemble the components. The tree search module optimizes the action sequence to achieve the most effective assembly. Through self-play and reinforcement learning, SAN learns to assemble components into complex structures. Our experiments demonstrate that SAN outperforms existing methods in terms of assembly quality and efficiency. Additionally, we showcase the versatility of SAN in various applications, including 3D shape generation, furniture arrangement, and urban planning. Our results indicate that SAN is a robust and efficient approach to spatial assembly, capable of generating intricate structures. We also demonstrate that the tradeoff can be mitigated by incorporating adversarial training into robot learning, which can improve both robustness and accuracy. Our findings are supported by experimental results on a simulated robotic manipulation task.
